extracted.intended_audience: registered patent attorneys/agents, USPTO disciplinary staff, and practitioners subject to USPTO ethics rules
extracted.subtask_short: USPTO disciplinary review for practitioner misconduct
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and procedural criteria used by the USPTO (OED and the Director) to evaluate attorney/agent misconduct and to determine appropriate disciplinary sanctions (including exclusion) in proceedings under 35 U.S.C. § 32 and 37 C.F.R. parts 10 and 11.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 10.23(a) - Disreputable or gross misconduct
rubrics_metrics.description: "A practitioner shall not engage in disreputable or gross misconduct."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Violations include deceiving a client to the client's injury (e.g., accepting fees for work not performed, failing to communicate, failing to file paid patent applications). The decision cites State ex rel. Oklahoma v. Raskin and OED precedent (e.g., In re Michael Shippey) as examples where accepting fees for unperformed work and failing to remit or communicate constituted gross misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 10.23(b)(4) - Dishonesty, fraud, deceit, or misrepresentation
rubrics_metrics.description: "A practitioner shall not ... engage in conduct involving dishonesty, fraud, deceit, or misrepresentation."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applies where a practitioner affirmatively represents to a client (by invoice, email, or statement) that an application was prepared/filed when it was not, or otherwise misrepresents matter status (e.g., claiming a patent-pending number). OED and case law (In re Riley, In re Muhammad, In re Kang, Matter of Trey T. Meyer) support that false statements about filing/status and billing for unperformed services violate this rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 10.23(c)(3) (via §§ 10.23(a),(b)) - Misappropriation or failure to remit funds to the Office
rubrics_metrics.description: Prohibits misappropriation of, or failure to properly or timely remit, funds received by a practitioner from a client to pay a fee which the client is required by law to pay to the Office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: billing/collecting specific USPTO filing fees (e.g., $565, $600) but failing to file the corresponding application and failing to forward those fees to the Office. OED precedent (In re Kang, Greiner) treats retaining funds intended for Office fees as a §10.23(c)(3) violation.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 10.77(c) - Neglect of a legal matter entrusted to the practitioner
rubrics_metrics.description: "A practitioner shall not ... neglect a legal matter entrusted to the practitioner."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Neglect is consistent failure or indifference to perform obligations (e.g., failing to prepare/file and prosecute patent applications after being hired and paid). Guidance/case law (Conroy, Freed; In re Riley, In re Muhammad) describe neglect as conscious disregard or routine failure to advance client interests; it is a serious ethical violation.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 10.84(a) - Failure to seek lawful objectives of a client
rubrics_metrics.description: "A practitioner shall not intentionally ... fail to seek the lawful objectives of a client through reasonably available means permitted by law and the Disciplinary Rules."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Violations occur where a practitioner intentionally fails to perform paid legal services (e.g., not filing paid applications), sends invoices for unperformed services, and accepts payment. Precedents (In re Riley; Cincinnati Bar Ass'n v. Lawrence; Disciplinary Counsel v. McShane) show such conduct breaches §10.84(a).

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.54(b) - Four-factor exclusion/sanction analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: When exclusion is considered, an adjudicator must consider four factors: (1) whether practitioner violated a duty (to client/public/legal system/profession); (2) whether practitioner acted intentionally, knowingly, or negligently; (3) amount of actual or potential injury caused; and (4) existence of aggravating or mitigating factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The ALJ must explain the reason for exclusion after weighing these factors. Examples in the decision: finding duty violated (lying to client), knowing misconduct (no claim of mistake), significant actual/potential injury ($35,225 loss, possible loss of patent rights), and aggravating factors (lack of participation, failure to return files).

rubrics_metrics.name: Summary judgment standard in USPTO disciplinary proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: Summary judgment is appropriate when the pleadings, affidavits, and discovery documents show no genuine issue of material fact and the moving party is entitled to judgment as a matter of law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nonmovant bears burden to show a genuine issue of material fact and may not rest on pleadings or conclusory allegations. Failure to oppose or proffer evidence permits summary judgment. The decision cites Anderson v. Liberty Lobby and instructs that 37 C.F.R. §11.55(b) treats unraised exceptions as waived.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of collateral estoppel (offensive) to establish facts from prior state judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: Under applicable state law (Texas, as cited), offensive collateral estoppel requires that (1) the facts were fully and fairly litigated in the first action, (2) the facts were essential to the prior judgment, and (3) the party against whom estoppel is asserted was a party in the first action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A default judgment can satisfy the "fully and fairly litigated" prong (e.g., guilty plea/default may be treated as full and fair). The decision applies the three-prong Fullerton/Mendez analysis and cites DeLeon re implicit issue preclusion. Failure to appeal/reconsider the state judgment strengthens estoppel.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.55 appellate/briefing requirements and Director review
rubrics_metrics.description: An appeal of an ALJ initial decision to the USPTO Director must be filed within 30 days and include an appellate brief complying with §11.55 (clear statement of disputed facts and points of law; statement of issues and argument with citation to the factual record; formatting requirements). The Director may conduct de novo review of the factual record and may affirm, reverse, modify, or remand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nonconforming briefs may be refused entry by the Director. Failure to file a compliant brief or to include required exceptions/arguments is an independent basis to deny or reject an appeal. See 37 C.F.R. §§11.55, 11.56(a), 11.55(f) and the decision's treatment of Respondent's deficient four-page appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural obligations and remedies following an exclusion order (notice, dissociation, reinstatement conditions)
rubrics_metrics.description: When exclusion is ordered, the Director must give notice under 37 C.F.R. §11.59 to state disciplinary agencies/courts and public; the USPTO may dissociate the practitioner's name from Customer Numbers/PKI certificates; practitioner shall not obtain/appear on Customer Numbers until reinstated; disciplined practitioner must comply with duties in §11.58.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are post-discipline obligations and administrative steps the Office applies after imposing exclusion; the Order lists specific operational and notice measures and conditions for reinstatement and compliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions and jurisprudential guidance for aggravating/mitigating considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Aggravating factors include lack of participation in proceedings, failure to accept responsibility, and repeated or knowing misconduct; mitigating factors would be participation, remediation, explanation, or evidence of mistake/illness if proven.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The ALJ identified Respondent's general non-participation and failure to return files as aggravating. The decision explains that absence of any proffer, explanation, or request for further proceedings weighs against mitigation; such considerations factor into the sanction determination under §11.54(b)(4).
